Initiated

/ih-NISH-ee-ay-tid/ — rhymes with visited · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To be initiated means to have begun, started, or set something in motion.

Within a month she had initiated a collection route that volunteers ran every Saturday, hauling sorted glass to a depot across town.

Worked Example

When her school's recycling program wasn't working, one student initiated a complete redesign, recruiting volunteers and establishing a sorting system in every classroom.

Initiated is more precise than 'started'—it captures the sense of deliberately making the choice to begin something new from your own decision, not just starting something that was already in motion. The student didn't just begin a recycling effort; she set an entirely new program in motion from her choice.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

launched: Launched means sent something out into the world with force and fanfare — a product launch, a rocket launch. Initiated is quieter and earlier: it means deliberately setting something in motion, often long before any public debut. An entrepreneur initiates a venture in a garage; she launches it with a press release.

spearheaded: Spearheaded means personally led an effort from the front, like the point of a spear, and implies ongoing leadership through the fight. Initiated only claims the start: whoever initiated a project set it in motion but may have handed it off the next day. Leading it forward is what spearheading adds.

commenced: Commenced is a formal, ceremonial word for began — proceedings commence, graduations commence. It marks a start without implying the starter created anything new. A judge commences a hearing that was already on the docket; the person who initiated the lawsuit set the whole matter in motion.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ended: brought something to its final close

abandoned: walked away, leaving it unfinished

Where it sits · how far from idea to real action — thought about → suggested → began → initiated

thought about vs. initiated: Thought about is far weaker than initiated: a student who only thought about a class newspaper produced a daydream, while initiating one means actually setting it in motion.

suggested vs. initiated: Suggesting a chess club at the library takes one sentence in a meeting; the person who initiated it booked the room, bought the boards, and made it real.

began vs. initiated: Began is weaker than initiated: a cashier begins her shift because the schedule says so, while initiating something goes further, deliberately setting a brand-new effort in motion yourself.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — init-

Root — init-: beginning, entrance — from Latin initium, literally in- ('into') + ire ('to go'): the going-in point

Suffix — -iate

Suffix — -iate: to make, to cause to be (forms verbs, as in graduate, activate)

Put it together

Put it together: Init- (beginning — from Latin initium, literally the 'going-in' point, from in- 'into' + ire 'to go') + -iate (to make, to cause) builds a verb meaning to cause something to begin, to set it in motion. The -d on the end is just the ordinary English past-tense ending, so all the word's history lives in 'initiate' itself. When you initiate something, you are quite literally stepping through the entrance and getting things going.

Use the root in a new word: initiative

Use the root in a new word: initiative: When volunteers wanted to clean the park, someone had to take the initiative and organize volunteers and set a date.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / neutral

Initiated is stronger and more purposeful than plain 'started.' Use initiated when someone makes a deliberate choice to begin something new, especially if they are taking charge. For routine or automatic starts, the simpler word 'began' often fits better.
